doc.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022

title: Recording the first play-a-longs with rhythm sections
summary: Rhythm players had to comp without soloing; Brubeck found it hard; Volume Six was recorded in New York.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Terrific story. And I wanted to speak about “So What” actually but a little later. Now we’ve got two laters. So this developed into this idea of recording a piano trio and assembling what you felt was enough information to get people started. Did you have trouble in a couple of things. First of all do you recall if the piano trio had to do some adjusting because they weren’t backing anybody up? They were just playing. Was that difficult for them at first?

In the early stages I don’t think it was because we all, none of us really knew what we were doing. We were trying to lay down some tracks and I probably told the piano player don’t play too busy. And drummer, don’t take a solo, delineate the form, eight bar

phrases, four bar phrases, whatever. And bass player, just walk. You know? And I don’t even think we did any bossa novas on the very, very first one. I doubt it. They were probably all kind of swing. But later, once we moved in and you had people like Hal Galper who you’ve interviewed, and some other ones, they found — Ronnie Mathews on the piano up in New York. They found it a little difficult to just comp. Dave Brubeck comped on my Dave Brubeck play-a-long. And afterwards he said, “Jamey, that’s the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.”
I can hear him say that.

Yeah. “Jamey, that’s the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.” I said, “What’s that?” He said, “Just to comp for five minutes like that.” But yes, so on some of those early ones I would scat sing. I’d have a microphone you know [scats]. And that seemed to free up the piano player. And if you listen on that Volume Six behind you there, if you listen carefully you can hear me playing the alto because that was my sixth play-a-long and that was the first one that I flew to New York to do with Kenny Barron and whoever it was, Ron Carter and Ben Riley. Yeah. And I played in the room but it seeped in somehow you know.
